India's GCCs are hiring - but not like before.

As AI reshapes roles across industries, global companies are becoming more selective, more deliberate, and more demanding about the kind of talent they're bringing in. The era of high-volume GCC hiring is giving way to something more targeted: specialists in AI, cybersecurity, and advanced tech capabilities that are increasingly hard to find and fiercely contested.
The numbers still tell an expansive story. By FY26, India is expected to be home to 2,117 GCCs - employing 2.36 million people and generating $100 billion in revenue. The foundation is strong. But the talent calculus is shifting fast.
"There's a lot of need around niche talents in the space of AI, cybersecurity," the newly appointed head of Daimler Truck Innovation Center India told Reuters. "It is difficult to find the right talent... it is challenging."
For GCC leaders, the challenge isn't ambition. It's execution - finding people with the right mix of technical expertise and adaptability in a market where everyone is looking for the same profiles.
The companies that crack this will define what the next chapter of India's GCC story looks like.

person_names: Pareekh Jain; Rohan Lobo; Tanya Pandey; Vikram Ahuja
content:
The data on Indian GCC leadership has been moving in one direction for a while now.

115 global roles in 2015. 6,500 today. 30,000 projected by 2030. And nearly 20% of GCCs now enjoying real strategic authority, up from just 5% a decade ago.

The nature of that work has changed too. Walmart manages its global retail technology from Bengaluru. Target runs its digital commerce and supply chain platform from here. Microsoft develops key parts of Azure in India. Amazon builds Alexa and Prime Video technology here. These are not support functions. They are core enterprise mandates,  owned and led from India.

But leadership is where the most important shift is happening. GCCs operating in global matrix environments are producing a new kind of leader, one who influences strategy across geographies and functions rather than relying on hierarchy. The centres that have moved fastest are the ones given a specific outcome to own from the start, rather than a broad mandate to innovate over time.

40-45% of centres still handle back-office and IT support. The gap between participation and ownership remains. But the direction is clear and the leaders coming out of India's GCC ecosystem are increasingly the ones shaping what global enterprises do next.

content:
29% of GCCs in India are already operating as true catalysts for enterprise-wide transformation.
That number should make every global business leader pause because it means 71% are not.
The gap between those two groups is not technology. It's not talent. It's not even budget. It's the willingness to reimagine what a GCC is actually for.

Most enterprises run on a strange contradiction. 

While the systems powering them evolve constantly, the documentation explaining how they work is almost always outdated.

In large financial organizations, that gap creates real operational risk. A regulatory change, a new product launch or even a small production issue can ripple across dozens of systems, integrations and workflows. Yet, understanding those dependencies often depends on fragmented documentation, or institutional memory sitting inside a handful of employees.

Fidelity International wanted a different approach.

The result is The Brain, an internal AI powered system designed to understand the operational truth of the enterprise directly from live implementation rather than static documentation. Instead of relying on manuals or process notes, the system reads application code, configurations, integrations and dependency graphs to create a continuously updated understanding of how systems actually operate.

“A business analyst can actually chat with the Brain to forward engineer the code for a new requirement or a changing requirement,” says Rohit Jetly.

Innovation doesn’t happen on tech islands anymore — it happens in networks.

At #ETGCC2025, the panel “Beyond Tech Islands: Engineering Synergies Across GCC Networks – Collaborate or Compete, Your Tech Future Depends on It” brought together leaders who are turning GCCs from isolated excellence centers into connected enterprise engines.

Key insights from the conversation

From projects to platforms
High-performing GCCs are moving away from one-off projects to platform-first models where data, products, and capabilities are built once and reused across businesses, markets, and functions.

GCCs as orchestrators, not order-takers
India hubs are increasingly acting as orchestrators of business outcomes—aligning engineering, data, security, and operations around shared OKRs instead of local success metrics.

Borderless innovation is the new baseline
Prototypes designed in India are now being tested, validated, and scaled globally, making GCC networks the default playground for experimentation, AI-native products, and faster time-to-market.

AI-native capability hubs by 2030
The shared vision: GCCs evolving into AI-native, enterprise-wide capability hubs—where 100% of roles touch AI in some way, 75% are human-augmented, and 25% are fully AI-driven.

content:
“AI that thinks was yesterday. AI that acts is where GCCs step in.”

At #ETGCC2025, the panel “Rewriting the Rules: AI that Acts, GCCs that Lead” brought together leaders who are not just talking about AI agents—but already wiring them into how global enterprises run.

Sudha KV, VP Software Engineering and ISG India Site Head, Dell Technologies
Harish Maheshwari, Director Finance system & Data, Thomson Reuters

Key insights from the conversation

Agentic AI is no longer theory. From Ericsson’s end-to-end, AI-orchestrated L&D workflows to Visa’s intelligent commerce and fraud models, GCCs are moving beyond POCs to production, with 30–60% efficiency gains and radically faster turnaround times.

The tech stack is only half the story. The panel dug into the real plumbing of AI-at-scale: GPU-heavy infra, data platforms, semantic layers, DevOps and MLOps, observability, and governance that acts like brakes on a race car—the very thing that lets you go faster with control.

But the sharpest shift is human. Transactional roles are giving way to DevOps thinkers, hybrid “AI + human” operators, citizen developers, and domain-led AI talent. The message was clear: AI will retire some tasks, but create entirely new careers—if leaders invest in upskilling and bring their people along.

content:
Speed means nothing if trust can’t keep up — and in today’s AI-fueled enterprise, security isn’t a checklist, it’s the chassis.

At #ETGCC2025, the panel “Cyber-First Thinking: Securing by Design, Agile by Default” brought together leaders who’ve lived the reality of transforming legacy systems, modernizing cloud architectures, and defending against threats that evolve faster than policies.

Featuring:
• Arundathi Rao, Vice President, Global IT India, Hewlett Packard Enterprise
• Kailash Maisekar, Country Director & India Board Member, Idox plc
Moderated by Saurabh Kumar, The Economic Times

Key insights from the conversation

Trust is the new transformation currency.
Whether it’s business stakeholders, boards, employees, or millions of end users—every digital shift succeeds only when trust is built in from the start, not bolted on at the end.

Zero trust isn’t a buzzword—it’s a survival model.
From legacy rewrites to cloud migrations, cyber has moved from a “later” step to a design principle, embedded across architecture, DevOps pipelines, and product life cycles.

Security is the brake that lets innovation accelerate.
Just like a high-speed car relies on great brakes, companies rely on cyber to move faster with confidence. Guardrails don’t slow transformation—they unlock it.

People are the strongest (and weakest) link.
Both panelists underscored the cultural shift: training teams to raise concerns early, rewarding vulnerability detection, and turning every employee into a proactive defender.
